lessons.title: Production Planning and Scheduling
lessons.body:
Production planning means deciding what to bake, how much, and when, so you meet customer demand without overbaking or running out. Start by tracking your daily sales for two weeks. Write down each item, quantity sold, and time of day. For example, if you sell 50 loaves of bread by 10 AM but only 10 after 2 PM, you know to bake 60 loaves early and maybe 20 more in the afternoon. Use a simple notebook or a chalkboard to record this. In many African bakeries, demand spikes on weekends, month-ends when people get paid, and holidays. Adjust your plan accordingly.

Next, create a weekly production schedule. List each product, the days you bake it, and the batch size. For instance, bake 100 mandazi every morning, 200 on Saturdays. Bake cakes only on order. Write this schedule on a large paper and hang it in the bakery. Your team can see what to do each day. Include prep time: dough for bread needs 1-2 hours to rise, so start at 4 AM to have fresh bread by 7 AM.

Calculate your capacity. How many loaves can your oven hold? If your oven fits 30 loaves and takes 45 minutes per batch, you can bake 30 loaves per hour. To bake 120 loaves, you need 4 hours. Plan your start time backwards from when you want bread ready. If you want bread at 6 AM, start baking at 2 AM. But you also need time for mixing, shaping, and proofing. So start mixing at 10 PM the night before. This is called backward scheduling.

Don't forget ingredient ordering. If you plan to bake 500 loaves this week, you need about 250 kg of flour (assuming 500g flour per loaf). Order flour, yeast, sugar, and oil in advance. Keep a buffer of 10% extra for unexpected orders or spoilage. In many African markets, supply can be unreliable, so having a week's stock is wise.

Finally, review your plan daily. Did you sell out? Did you throw away bread? Adjust tomorrow's batch. After a month, you'll have a reliable rhythm that reduces waste and increases profit.

lessons.title: Workflow Optimization in the Bakery
lessons.body:
Workflow optimization means arranging your bakery so that work moves smoothly from one step to the next without delays or wasted motion. Imagine your bakery as a river: ingredients flow in, become dough, then bread, then out to customers. If the river has rocks (bottlenecks), work slows down. Your job is to remove those rocks.

First, map your current process. Write down every step from receiving flour to selling bread. For example: 1) Store flour, 2) Weigh ingredients, 3) Mix dough, 4) Knead, 5) Proof, 6) Shape, 7) Bake, 8) Cool, 9) Package, 10) Sell. Now, for each step, note how long it takes and who does it. You might find that mixing takes 20 minutes but shaping takes 45 minutes because only one person does it. That's a bottleneck. Train another worker to shape, or buy a simple dough divider.

Next, arrange your equipment in the order of the process. If your mixer is far from the oven, workers carry heavy dough across the room, wasting time and energy. Place the mixer next to the shaping table, and the shaping table next to the oven. Use shelves and carts to move items. In small African bakeries, a simple wooden table on wheels can save hours.

Reduce unnecessary steps. Do you sift flour twice? Once is enough. Do you wash bowls between every batch? Maybe you can scrape and reuse for the same type of dough. But never compromise hygiene. Also, combine tasks: while dough proofs, start mixing the next batch. This is called parallel processing.

Standardize tools. Have the same size bowls, measuring cups, and baking trays. This reduces confusion and speeds up work. Label everything. Use a permanent marker to write '1 kg flour' on a container.

Finally, involve your workers. Ask them what slows them down. They often have the best ideas. For example, a baker might suggest moving the cooling rack closer to the packaging table. Implement one improvement per week. Over time, your bakery will run like a well-oiled machine, producing more with less effort.

lessons.title: Batch Production vs. Made-to-Order
lessons.body:
In baking, you can produce in batches (make many identical items at once) or made-to-order (make only what a customer orders). Each has pros and cons. Your choice depends on your products, customer demand, and capacity.

Batch production is best for items that sell quickly and have a long shelf life, like bread, mandazi, or biscuits. You bake 100 loaves at once, which lowers cost per loaf because you use less fuel and labor per unit. For example, baking 100 loaves might take 2 hours of labor and 3 hours of oven time. Baking 10 loaves separately would take almost the same time, making each loaf more expensive. Batch production also allows you to offer lower prices and attract more customers. However, you risk waste if you bake more than you sell. So track sales and bake slightly less than you expect to sell, then adjust.

Made-to-order is best for custom cakes, special pastries, or large orders for events. You bake only when a customer orders and often require a deposit. This eliminates waste because you know exactly what to make. But it requires more planning and communication. You must agree on design, flavor, and pickup time. For example, a wedding cake might take 6 hours to bake and decorate. You need to schedule it around your regular bread production. Made-to-order can be more profitable because customers pay a premium for customization.

You can combine both. For instance, bake bread in batches every morning, but take custom cake orders for weekends. Use a whiteboard to list orders and their due dates. Assign one person to handle custom orders so they don't disrupt the main production line.

In many African bakeries, the sweet spot is 80% batch production of daily staples and 20% made-to-order for higher-margin items. This balances steady cash flow with profitable specials. Always calculate your cost per item for both methods. If a batch loaf costs 30 cents to make and sells for 60 cents, you make 30 cents profit. A custom cake might cost $5 to make and sell for $15, giving $10 profit. But custom cakes take more time, so don't overcommit.

Review your sales weekly. If a batch item isn't selling, reduce batch size or switch to made-to-order. If custom orders are booming, train more staff. Stay flexible.

lessons.title: Quality Assurance in Baking
lessons.body:
Quality assurance means setting standards for your products and checking them at every step so customers get the same good bread every time. Without quality control, one day your bread is great, the next day it's burnt or dense. Customers notice and stop buying.

Start by defining what 'good' means for each product. For bread: golden brown crust, soft inside, even shape, weighs 500g. For mandazi: fluffy, not greasy, uniform size. Write these standards on a poster and hang it in the bakery. Train your workers to check against these standards.

Use simple tools to measure. A kitchen scale ensures each loaf weighs the same. A thermometer checks water temperature for yeast (too hot kills yeast, too cold slows it). For bread, the internal temperature should be around 90Â°C when done. A timer prevents overbaking. Keep a logbook: record batch number, date, who baked, and any issues. This helps trace problems.

Check ingredients when they arrive. Smell the flour for mustiness. Check yeast expiry date. If yeast is old, your dough won't rise. Store ingredients properly: flour in airtight containers off the floor, yeast in the fridge. In humid African climates, moisture ruins flour quickly.

During production, do spot checks. After mixing, feel the dough: it should be smooth and elastic. After proofing, it should double in size. After baking, cut one loaf to check crumb. If it's dense, maybe you didn't proof long enough or yeast was weak. Adjust next batch.

Hygiene is part of quality. Workers must wash hands, wear clean aprons, and tie hair back. Clean benches with food-safe sanitizer. Customers equate cleanliness with quality.

Finally, get customer feedback. Ask regulars if they noticed any change. If they complain, investigate immediately. A simple 'How was the bread today?' can catch issues early. Remember, quality assurance is not a one-time event; it's a daily habit. It builds trust and loyal customers who return because they know what to expect.

lessons.title: Waste Reduction Strategies
lessons.body:
Waste in a bakery eats your profit. Every loaf you throw away is money lost. But with simple strategies, you can reduce waste to under 5% of production.

First, track your waste. Keep a 'waste log' where you record what was thrown away, how much, and why. Maybe you baked too much, or bread burned, or dough over-proofed. After a week, you'll see patterns. For example, if you throw away 10 loaves every Monday, maybe Monday sales are slow. So bake less on Mondays.

Second, improve your sales forecasting. Use historical data: last week you sold 200 loaves on Saturday, so bake 210 this Saturday. But if there's a funeral or festival, demand may spike. Ask customers about upcoming events. Also, consider the weather: rainy days may reduce foot traffic.

Third, use day-old bread creatively. Don't throw it away. Turn it into breadcrumbs, croutons, or pudding. Sell day-old bread at a discount. In many African communities, day-old bread is still good for making porridge or as animal feed. You can even partner with a local farmer who buys stale bread for pigs.

Fourth, reduce production errors. Train workers to measure ingredients accurately. Over-kneading or under-proofing ruins batches. Use timers and scales. If a batch is slightly imperfect but still safe, sell it as 'special' at a lower price rather than discarding.

Fifth, manage ingredients well. Store flour in a cool, dry place. Use FIFO (First In, First Out): use older stock first. Rotate shelves. Buy in bulk only if you can use it before it spoils. For perishables like eggs and milk, buy smaller quantities more often.

Sixth, optimize your baking schedule. Bake in batches that match demand. If you sell 50 loaves in the morning and 30 in the evening, bake 50 early and 30 later, not 80 all at once. This reduces stale bread.

Finally, involve your team. Offer a small bonus if waste stays below 3% for a month. When workers know waste is money, they become careful. A bakery that wastes less earns more and can lower prices, attracting more customers.

lessons.title: Implementing Standard Operating Procedures
lessons.body:
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) are written steps for how to do a task the same way every time. They ensure consistency, train new workers quickly, and reduce mistakes. In a bakery, SOPs cover everything from opening the shop to baking bread to cleaning.

Start by identifying tasks that need an SOP. Focus on critical ones: mixing dough, baking bread, scaling ingredients, and cleaning. Don't try to write SOPs for everything at once. Begin with your best-selling product. For example, 'SOP for White Bread' might include: 1) Weigh 1 kg flour, 600 ml water, 10 g yeast, 15 g salt, 20 g sugar. 2) Mix dry ingredients. 3) Add water, mix 10 minutes. 4) Knead 15 minutes. 5) Proof 1 hour. 6) Shape into 2 loaves. 7) Proof 45 minutes. 8) Bake at 200Â°C for 30 minutes. 9) Cool on rack.

Write each step in simple language. Use numbers and bullet points. Include what tools are needed. Add a photo if possible. For example, show what the dough should look like after kneading. Keep the SOP in a plastic sleeve so it doesn't get dirty. Hang it near the work area.

Train your workers on the SOP. Demonstrate each step. Then let them do it while you watch. Correct mistakes gently. Have them sign a sheet saying they've been trained. This is important for accountability.

Review SOPs regularly. If you find a better way, update the SOP. Date each version. For instance, 'SOP for Bread, Version 2, 1 March 2025.' Old versions should be removed to avoid confusion.

SOPs also help with food safety. Include handwashing, sanitizing surfaces, and proper storage. For example, 'SOP for Cleaning: 1) Scrape benches. 2) Wipe with soapy water. 3) Spray with food-safe sanitizer. 4) Air dry.'

Finally, use SOPs to onboard new staff. Instead of explaining everything verbally, give them the SOP folder. They can read and follow. This saves you time and ensures quality. In busy African bakeries, SOPs are the backbone of consistency. They turn a chaotic kitchen into a professional operation.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Production & Operations Management for African Bakeries

This practical reference consolidates the operational tools you need to run a bakery in an African market: how to plan production, optimise workflow, choose between batch and made-to-order models, protect quality, cut waste, and institutionalise standard operating procedures (SOPs). It is written for owner-managers of small and medium bakeriesâfrom a one-oven shop in Kumasi to a 20-staff operation supplying supermarkets in Nairobi. Every recommendation is designed to protect margin, because in baking, margin is won or lost on the production floor, not in the shop.

African bakeries face a distinctive operating environment: intermittent power, volatile flour and sugar prices, informal distribution, thin cold-chain, and demand spikes around festive seasons (Christmas, Eid, Easter) and school terms. Your operations system must be resilient to these realities, not copied blindly from European textbooks.

1. Production Planning and Scheduling

Production planning answers three questions daily: what to bake, how much, and when. Start with a demand forecast built from the last 4â8 weeks of sales, adjusted for day-of-week patterns (weekends and Mondays typically peak), payday cycles, and known events. Convert that forecast into a daily production schedule by working backwards from the moment product must be on the shelf.

For a bakery selling bread at 06:00 and pastries at 08:00, the schedule is a countdown: dough mixing at 02:00, bulk fermentation 02:30â04:00, shaping 04:00â05:00, proofing 05:00â05:40, baking 05:40â06:00. Post this schedule on the wall; verbal plans collapse under pressure.

2. Workflow Optimisation in the Bakery

Workflow optimisation eliminates the three wastes that kill bakery throughput: motion (staff walking to fetch ingredients), waiting (ovens idle while dough proofs), and transport (finished goods crossing the production area). Arrange the bakery in a U-shape or straight line following the dough: storage â weighing â mixing â fermentation â shaping â proofing â baking â cooling â packing â dispatch.

Keep ingredients within arm's reach of the mixing station. Place cooling racks adjacent to the oven, never across the room. In many African bakeries, the single biggest gain comes from separating the "hot" zone (ovens) from the "cold" zone (proofing, packing) so staff are not constantly crossing paths.

3. Batch Production vs. Made-to-Order

Batch productionâbaking standard loaves, rolls, and pastries in fixed quantitiesâgives you economies of scale, predictable labour, and lower per-unit cost. Made-to-order (custom cakes, event breads, specialty items) gives you higher margin per unit but requires flexible scheduling and skilled labour. Most African bakeries should run a hybrid model: 70â85% batch production for daily bread and snacks, 15â30% made-to-order for cakes, catering, and premium items.

Table 1: Batch vs. Made-to-Order â Decision Matrix
Factor Batch Production Made-to-Order
Typical productsBread, rolls, scones, meat piesCakes, wedding breads, catering
Lead timeSame day / overnight24â72 hours notice
Gross margin20â35%45â65%
Labour skillSemi-skilledSkilled / specialist
Waste riskHigh if forecast is wrongLow (paid deposit)
Cash flowDaily salesDeposit upfront, balance on delivery

Source: Adapted from FAO, Small-Scale Cereal Milling and Baking (Agricultural Services Bulletin 138, 2001), and ILO, Small-Scale Baking Technical Memorandum No. 5 (1986).

4. Quality Assurance in Baking

Quality assurance (QA) in a bakery has four anchors: ingredient control, process control, product testing, and traceability. Weigh ingredients every batchânever "eyeball" flour or yeast. Record oven temperature and baking time for every bake. Check dough temperature after mixing (ideally 24â26Â°C for straight dough). Reject flour with off-smell, lumps, or weevil damage before it enters the mixer.

In many African markets, food safety regulators (e.g., NAFDAC in Nigeria, KEBS in Kenya, FDA Ghana) require basic hygiene and labelling compliance. Build these into your SOPs from day oneâretrofitting compliance is far more expensive.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Oven & Dough Safety

Bakery ovens operate at 180â250Â°C and are the leading cause of workplace burns. Never allow staff to reach into a hot oven without heat-resistant gloves and a full-length apron. Ensure gas ovens are leak-tested monthly; LPG leaks are a major cause of bakery fires in urban Africa. Dough mixers with exposed belts or gears must have guards fittedâentanglement injuries are common where second-hand equipment is imported without safety covers. Keep a dry-powder fire extinguisher within 5 metres of every oven and train at least two staff per shift to use it. First-aid kit must include burn gel, not just plasters.

5. Waste Reduction Strategies

Bakery waste typically runs 5â15% of production in African SMEsâmostly from over-baking, stale returns, and ingredient spoilage. The financial impact is severe: at a 10% waste rate and 30% gross margin, you are losing roughly a third of your profit.

Table 2: Common Bakery Waste Sources and Countermeasures
Waste Source Typical Loss Countermeasure
Over-production of bread4â8%Track daily sell-through; bake in two waves (early + midday)
Stale / unsold returns3â6%Convert to breadcrumbs, croutons, or day-old discount shelf
Ingredient spoilage1â3%FIFO stock rotation; airtight containers; pest control
Dough over-mixing / scaling errors1â2%Digital scales; standard recipes; staff training
Power-related spoilageVariableBackup generator or inverter; cold-room temperature log

Source: Compiled from FAO (2001) and ILO (1986) small-scale baking guidance, with field benchmarks from African SME bakery assessments.

6. Implementing Standard Operating Procedures

An SOP is a written instruction that lets any trained staff member produce the same result. In a bakery, you need SOPs for at least: (1) receiving and storing ingredients; (2) dough mixing and fermentation; (3) baking and cooling; (4) cleaning and sanitation; (5) cash and stock reconciliation. Keep each SOP to one page, in the language your staff read most comfortably, with photos where possible.

Implementation follows a simple cycle: write â train â observe â correct â re-train. Do not write twenty SOPs at once. Start with the two that matter mostâusually mixing and bakingâand add one per month. Post them at the workstation, not in an office file.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Daily production plan posted on the wall before the first shift starts.
  • â All ingredients weighed on digital scalesâno eyeballing.
  • â Oven temperature and bake time logged for every batch.
  • â Workflow follows the dough; no backtracking across the production floor.
  • â Sell-through rate reviewed weekly; over-production trimmed by 5%.
  • â Stale bread converted to crumbs or discounted, never binned without record.
  • â Fire extinguisher and burn kit checked monthly; two trained staff per shift.
  • â At least two SOPs written, posted, and trained in the last 90 days.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-Scale Cereal Milling and Baking (Agricultural Services Bulletin 138)
  • ILO â Small-Scale Baking (Technical Memorandum No. 5)
  • FAO â Food Wastage Footprint & Reduction Strategies
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (food safety for small food businesses)
  • African Development Bank â SME Development Resources

This module is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills programme â Bakery Business track. Use it alongside your local regulator's food safety requirements and your own sales data.

quiz.q: What is the first step in production planning?
options: B) Track daily sales for two weeks
quiz.explanation: Tracking sales helps you understand demand patterns before planning production.

quiz.q: If your oven fits 30 loaves and takes 45 minutes per batch, how many loaves can you bake in 3 hours?
quiz.explanation: 3 hours = 180 minutes. 180/45 = 4 batches. 4 x 30 = 120 loaves.

quiz.q: What is backward scheduling?
options: A) Scheduling from the end time back to the start
C) Scheduling from start to finish
quiz.explanation: Backward scheduling starts with the desired finish time and works backwards to determine when to begin.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a 10% buffer of ingredients?
options: B) For unexpected orders or spoilage
quiz.explanation: A buffer covers unexpected demand or ingredient loss, preventing production stoppage.

quiz.q: How often should you review your production plan?
quiz.explanation: Daily review allows quick adjustments to batch sizes based on actual sales.

quiz.q: What is a bottleneck in bakery workflow?
options: B) A step that slows down the whole process
quiz.explanation: A bottleneck is any step that limits overall production speed.

quiz.q: Which of these is a way to optimize workflow?
options: A) Place mixer far from oven
B) Arrange equipment in order of process
D) Do tasks one by one
quiz.explanation: Arranging equipment in process order reduces movement and time waste.

quiz.q: What is parallel processing?
options: A) Doing two tasks at the same time
B) Doing tasks in a straight line
D) Hiring two people for one task
quiz.explanation: Parallel processing means performing multiple tasks simultaneously to save time.

quiz.q: Why should you standardize tools?
options: B) To reduce confusion and speed up work
quiz.explanation: Standard tools ensure consistency and efficiency in production.

quiz.q: Who often has the best ideas for workflow improvement?
quiz.explanation: Workers perform the tasks daily and notice inefficiencies first-hand.

quiz.q: Batch production is best for which type of product?
quiz.explanation: Batch production suits high-demand, shelf-stable items like bread.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of batch production?
options: B) Risk of waste if unsold
quiz.explanation: If you bake more than you sell, unsold items become waste.

quiz.q: Made-to-order production is best for:
quiz.explanation: Custom cakes require specific designs and are made only when ordered.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of made-to-order?
quiz.explanation: Since you only make what is ordered, there is no unsold product waste.

quiz.q: In many African bakeries, what is a recommended mix of batch and made-to-order?
quiz.explanation: 80% batch ensures steady cash flow, while 20% made-to-order adds higher margins.

quiz.q: What does quality assurance ensure?
quiz.explanation: Quality assurance sets standards and checks to deliver the same good product every time.

quiz.q: What tool ensures each loaf weighs the same?
quiz.explanation: A kitchen scale measures weight accurately for uniform loaves.

quiz.q: What internal temperature should bread reach when done?
quiz.explanation: Bread is fully baked when its internal temperature is around 90Â°C.

quiz.q: Why is hygiene part of quality assurance?
options: A) It makes bread taste better
B) Customers equate cleanliness with quality
quiz.explanation: Cleanliness signals quality and safety, building customer trust.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer complains about bread quality?
quiz.explanation: Investigating complaints helps identify and fix quality issues quickly.

quiz.q: What is the first step to reduce waste?
quiz.explanation: Tracking waste reveals patterns and causes, enabling targeted reductions.

quiz.q: What is FIFO?
quiz.explanation: FIFO means using older stock first to prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: How can you use day-old bread?
quiz.explanation: Day-old bread can be repurposed into breadcrumbs, croutons, or pudding.

quiz.q: What is a good target for waste percentage?
quiz.explanation: With good strategies, bakeries can reduce waste to under 5%.

quiz.q: How can you motivate workers to reduce waste?
options: B) Offer a bonus for low waste
quiz.explanation: A bonus ties their effort to savings, encouraging careful work.

quiz.q: What does SOP stand for?
quiz.explanation: SOP stands for Standard Operating Procedure.

quiz.q: Why are SOPs important?
options: B) They ensure consistency and train new workers
D) They are only for large bakeries
quiz.explanation: SOPs provide written steps for consistent quality and easy training.

quiz.q: What should an SOP for bread include?
options: B) Ingredients, steps, tools, and times
quiz.explanation: A complete SOP covers ingredients, steps, tools, and timings.

quiz.q: How often should SOPs be reviewed?
options: B) Regularly and updated if needed
quiz.explanation: Regular review ensures SOPs reflect best practices and remain effective.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using SOPs for onboarding?
options: A) Saves time and ensures quality
quiz.explanation: New staff can read and follow SOPs, reducing training time and maintaining quality.
